text:
Below is a practical threat-hunting approach for suspicious Windows Scheduled Task creation using Windows Security events such as `4688` process creation and `4698` scheduled task creation.

---

## 1. Sigma and Splunk Detection Logic

### Sigma: Suspicious Scheduled Task Creation via `schtasks.exe`

```yaml
title: Suspicious Scheduled Task Creation With Script or LOLBin Execution
id: 6a2d8d7e-6b1e-4db8-b2a0-suspicious-schtasks-create
status: experimental
description: Detects suspicious scheduled task creation using schtasks.exe to execute PowerShell, scripts, or binaries from user-writable locations.
author: example
date: 2026/06/05
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_schtasks:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/Create'
      - '/create'
  selection_suspicious_exec:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'powershell'
      - 'pwsh'
      - 'cmd.exe'
      - 'wscript'
      - 'cscript'
      - 'mshta'
      - 'rundll32'
      - 'regsvr32'
      - 'bitsadmin'
      - 'certutil'
      - 'curl'
      - 'wget'
      - '.ps1'
      - '.vbs'
      - '.js'
      - '.jse'
      - '.hta'
      - '.bat'
      - '.cmd'
  selection_user_writable:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '\Users\Public\'
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
      - '\Windows\Temp\'
      - 'C:\Users\'
  condition: selection_schtasks and selection_suspicious_exec and selection_user_writable
fields:
  - UtcTime
  - User
  - Image
  - ParentImage
  - CommandLine
  - ParentCommandLine
  - Computer
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate software updaters
  - Enterprise software deployment tools
  - Admin-created maintenance tasks
  - Security tools creating recurring tasks
level: high
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1053.005
```

---

### Sigma: Suspicious Windows Event ID 4698 Scheduled Task Registration

```yaml
title: Suspicious Scheduled Task Registered With Script Interpreter Or User-Writable Path
id: e90d9a1c-39d4-47cc-9c0e-suspicious-4698-task
status: experimental
description: Detects suspicious Windows scheduled task registration where the task action executes scripting engines or files from user-writable locations.
author: example
date: 2026/06/05
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection_event:
    EventID: 4698
  selection_interpreter:
    TaskContent|contains:
      - '<Command>powershell.exe</Command>'
      - '<Command>pwsh.exe</Command>'
      - '<Command>cmd.exe</Command>'
      - '<Command>wscript.exe</Command>'
      - '<Command>cscript.exe</Command>'
      - '<Command>mshta.exe</Command>'
      - '<Command>rundll32.exe</Command>'
      - '<Command>regsvr32.exe</Command>'
      - '<Command>bitsadmin.exe</Command>'
      - '<Command>certutil.exe</Command>'
  selection_script_or_path:
    TaskContent|contains:
      - '.ps1'
      - '.vbs'
      - '.js'
      - '.jse'
      - '.hta'
      - '.bat'
      - '.cmd'
      - '\Users\Public\'
      - '\AppData\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
      - '\Windows\Temp\'
  condition: selection_event and selection_interpreter and selection_script_or_path
fields:
  - EventID
  - Computer
  - SubjectUserName
  - SubjectDomainName
  - TaskName
  - TaskContent
falsepositives:
  - IT automation
  - Software update tasks
  - Administrative maintenance scripts
  - Endpoint management agents
level: high
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1053.005
```

---

### Splunk Detection: `schtasks.exe` Process Creation

```spl
index=windows sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4688
| eval Image=coalesce(New_Process_Name, Image)
| eval CommandLine=coalesce(Process_Command_Line, CommandLine)
| where like(lower(Image), "%\\schtasks.exe")
| where match(lower(CommandLine), "(^|\\s)/create\\b")
| where match(lower(CommandLine), "powershell|pwsh|cmd\\.exe|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|bitsadmin|certutil|curl|wget|\\.ps1|\\.vbs|\\.js|\\.jse|\\.hta|\\.bat|\\.cmd")
| where match(lower(CommandLine), "\\\\users\\\\public\\\\|\\\\appdata\\\\|\\\\temp\\\\|\\\\programdata\\\\|\\\\windows\\\\temp\\\\|c:\\\\users\\\\")
| table _time host user Parent_Process_Name Image CommandLine
```

---

### Splunk Detection: Event ID 4698 Suspicious Scheduled Task Registration

```spl
index=windows sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4698
| eval task_content=lower(Task_Content)
| eval task_name=coalesce(Task_Name, TaskName)
| where match(task_content, "powershell\\.exe|pwsh\\.exe|cmd\\.exe|wscript\\.exe|cscript\\.exe|mshta\\.exe|rundll32\\.exe|regsvr32\\.exe|bitsadmin\\.exe|certutil\\.exe")
| where match(task_content, "\\.ps1|\\.vbs|\\.js|\\.jse|\\.hta|\\.bat|\\.cmd|\\\\users\\\\public\\\\|\\\\appdata\\\\|\\\\temp\\\\|\\\\programdata\\\\|\\\\windows\\\\temp\\\\")
| table _time host SubjectUserName SubjectDomainName task_name Task_Content
```

---

### Combined Splunk Hunt: Correlate `4688` and `4698`

```spl
(
  search index=windows sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4688
  | eval src_type="process_creation"
  | eval Image=coalesce(New_Process_Name, Image)
  | eval CommandLine=coalesce(Process_Command_Line, CommandLine)
  | where like(lower(Image), "%\\schtasks.exe")
  | where match(lower(CommandLine), "(^|\\s)/create\\b")
  | eval task_hint=lower(CommandLine)
  | table _time host user src_type Image CommandLine task_hint
)
OR
(
  search index=windows sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4698
  | eval src_type="task_registered"
  | eval task_hint=lower(coalesce(Task_Name, TaskName))
  | table _time host SubjectUserName SubjectDomainName src_type task_hint Task_Content
)
| sort host _time
```

You can then enrich or join by host, user, and time window.

---

## 2. Suspicious Command-Line Patterns

Look for scheduled tasks that launch interpreters, downloaders, proxy execution binaries, or payloads from user-writable locations.

### Suspicious `schtasks.exe` switches

```text
/Create
/SC MINUTE
/SC HOURLY
/MO 1
/MO 5
/MO 10
/MO 30
/RU SYSTEM
/RU "NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM"
/RL HIGHEST
/F
/TN legitimate-looking-name
/TR suspicious-action
```

### Suspicious task actions

```text
/TR "powershell.exe ..."
/TR "pwsh.exe ..."
/TR "cmd.exe /c ..."
/TR "wscript.exe ..."
/TR "cscript.exe ..."
/TR "mshta.exe ..."
/TR "rundll32.exe ..."
/TR "regsvr32.exe ..."
/TR "bitsadmin ..."
/TR "certutil ..."
```

### Suspicious PowerShell patterns

```text
-EncodedCommand
-enc
-e
-ExecutionPolicy Bypass
-ep bypass
-WindowStyle Hidden
-w hidden
-NoProfile
-nop
-NonInteractive
-noni
-File C:\Users\Public\*.ps1
-IEX
Invoke-Expression
DownloadString
DownloadFile
Invoke-WebRequest
iwr
curl
wget
Start-Process
```

### Suspicious paths

```text
C:\Users\Public\
C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\
C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp\
C:\Windows\Temp\
C:\ProgramData\
C:\Temp\
%TEMP%
%APPDATA%
%PUBLIC%
```

### Suspicious file extensions

```text
.ps1
.bat
.cmd
.vbs
.vbe
.js
.jse
.hta
.dll
.exe from user-writable directories
```

### Suspicious task names

Adversaries often use names that mimic legitimate software:

```text
AdobeUpdateTask
GoogleUpdateTask
ChromeUpdate
OneDriveUpdate
WindowsUpdate
MicrosoftEdgeUpdate
SecurityHealth
SystemCheck
Telemetry
OfficeUpdate
```

A legitimate-looking name is not enough for detection, but it is suspicious when paired with risky command content or unusual paths.

---

## 3. MITRE ATT&CK Mapping

Primary mapping:

| Technique | ID | Relevance |
|---|---:|---|
| Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task | `T1053.005` | Creation of Windows scheduled task for persistence or execution |
| Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell | `T1059.001` | Task executes `powershell.exe` or `.ps1` |
| Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell | `T1059.003` | Task executes `cmd.exe`, `.bat`, or `.cmd` |
| Windows Management Instrumentation / other execution | `T1047` | If task creation is performed remotely through WMI or management tooling |
| Ingress Tool Transfer | `T1105` | If the task downloads payloads using PowerShell, `certutil`, `bitsadmin`, `curl`, or `wget` |
| Masquerading | `T1036` | Task name mimics legitimate updater or Microsoft component |
| Proxy Execution | `T1218` | If task launches `mshta`, `rundll32`, `regsvr32`, etc. |
| Boot or Logon Autostart Execution | `T1547` | Related persistence category, though scheduled task-specific mapping should remain `T1053.005` |

Most important ATT&CK tag:

```text
T1053.005 - Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
```

---

## 4. Likely False Positives

Common benign sources include:

1. **Software updaters**
   - Adobe, Google, Microsoft Edge, Zoom, Teams, Java, Chrome, Firefox, printer software.

2. **Enterprise management tools**
   - SCCM/MECM, Intune, Tanium, BigFix, PDQ Deploy, Kaseya, NinjaOne, ConnectWise, Datto RMM.

3. **Security products**
   - EDR/AV agents creating maintenance, scan, or remediation tasks.

4. **Admin automation**
   - PowerShell scripts scheduled by IT admins for cleanup, inventory, backups, reporting, or patching.

5. **Backup and monitoring agents**
   - Veeam, Acronis, Datto, PRTG, SolarWinds, Splunk Universal Forwarder maintenance tasks.

6. **OS or application maintenance**
   - Legitimate Windows scheduled tasks under `\Microsoft\Windows\...`.

7. **Developer or lab machines**
   - Local scheduled scripts for build jobs, testing, or maintenance.

False positives are more likely when the task action points to a known signed binary in `Program Files` or `System32` and is created by a known management account or deployment tool.

---

## 5. Tuning and Enrichment Recommendations

### Tuning ideas

1. **Allowlist known good task names**
   - Example:
     - `\Microsoft\Windows\*`
     - `GoogleUpdateTaskMachineCore`
     - `GoogleUpdateTaskMachineUA`
     - `Adobe Acrobat Update Task`
     - Known EDR or RMM task names.

2. **Allowlist known good creators**
   - Domain admin automation accounts.
   - SCCM or Intune service accounts.
   - EDR management service accounts.

3. **Allowlist expected parent processes**
   - Example:
     - `CcmExec.exe`
     - `IntuneManagementExtension.exe`
     - Known RMM agent binaries.
     - EDR agent processes.

4. **Increase severity for user-writable paths**
   - `C:\Users\Public\`
   - `%APPDATA%`
   - `%TEMP%`
   - `C:\Windows\Temp\`
   - `C:\ProgramData\`

5. **Increase severity for encoded or hidden PowerShell**
   - `-EncodedCommand`
   - `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass`
   - `-WindowStyle Hidden`
   - `IEX`
   - `DownloadString`

6. **Increase severity for high-privilege tasks**
   - `/RU SYSTEM`
   - `/RL HIGHEST`
   - Task principal set to `SYSTEM`
   - Task configured to run whether user is logged on or not.

7. **Increase severity for high-frequency triggers**
   - `/SC MINUTE`
   - `/MO 1`
   - `/MO 5`
   - Repeats every few minutes.

8. **Increase severity for suspicious task names**
   - Names mimicking well-known vendors but pointing to unusual paths.

9. **Reduce noise from known signed binaries**
   - If the task runs a signed vendor binary from `C:\Program Files\Vendor\...`, lower severity.

10. **Require multiple suspicious conditions**
   - Example:
     - `schtasks /create`
     - plus interpreter execution
     - plus user-writable path
     - plus high frequency or elevated run level.

---

### Enrichment fields to add

Add these fields to the alert when possible:

| Enrichment | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Parent process | Shows whether task was created by installer, RMM, shell, Office, browser, etc. |
| Creator user SID and username | Determines whether normal user, admin, service account, or SYSTEM |
| Task XML content | Reveals command, arguments, triggers, principal, run level |
| Target command hash | Allows reputation checking |
| File signature status | Signed vs unsigned payload |
| File creation time | Recently dropped files are suspicious |
| File path reputation | User-writable paths are higher risk |
| Process ancestry | Helps identify initial access vector |
| Network connections near creation time | Identifies download/C2 behavior |
| DNS queries near execution time | Identifies suspicious domains |
| Endpoint risk score | Prior alerts on the same host/user |
| Asset criticality | Domain controllers, servers, executives’ laptops warrant higher severity |
| User context | Interactive user, service account, admin account |
| Logon session | Correlate with RDP, WinRM, PsExec, VPN, or local logon |

---

## 6. Recommended Investigation Steps

When this alert fires, investigate both the scheduled task and the process that created it.

### Step 1: Confirm task details

On the host, collect task configuration:

```cmd
schtasks /Query /TN "AdobeUpdateTask" /V /FO LIST
```

Or PowerShell:

```powershell
Get-ScheduledTask -TaskName "AdobeUpdateTask" | Format-List *
Get-ScheduledTaskInfo -TaskName "AdobeUpdateTask"
```

Export full task XML:

```powershell
Export-ScheduledTask -TaskName "AdobeUpdateTask"
```

Review:

- Task name
- Author
- Creation time
- Trigger frequency
- Run user
- Run level
- Action command
- Arguments
- Working directory

---

### Step 2: Review process creation telemetry

Look for the creation command:

```text
schtasks /Create ...
```

Key questions:

- Who created the task?
- Was the creator an expected admin or service account?
- What parent process launched `schtasks.exe`?
- Was it launched from:
  - `cmd.exe`
  - `powershell.exe`
  - `wscript.exe`
  - Office process
  - browser process
  - RMM tool
  - unknown executable?

Suspicious examples:

```text
winword.exe -> powershell.exe -> schtasks.exe
explorer.exe -> cmd.exe -> schtasks.exe
wscript.exe -> schtasks.exe
unknown.exe -> schtasks.exe
```

---

### Step 3: Inspect the task payload

For your example:

```text
powershell.exe -File C:\Users\Public\update.ps1
```

Investigate:

```powershell
Get-Item "C:\Users\Public\update.ps1" | Format-List *
Get-FileHash "C:\Users\Public\update.ps1"
Get-AuthenticodeSignature "C:\Users\Public\update.ps1"
```

Review contents carefully:

```powershell
Get-Content "C:\Users\Public\update.ps1"
```

Look for:

- Obfuscation
- Base64 encoded commands
- Network downloads
- Credential theft
- Reverse shell behavior
- Persistence modification
- AV/EDR tampering
- Lateral movement commands

---

### Step 4: Check whether the task executed

Review scheduled task operational logs:

```text
Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational
```

Useful event IDs include:

| Event ID | Meaning |
|---:|---|
| 106 | Task registered |
| 140 | Task updated |
| 200 | Action started |
| 201 | Action completed |
| 129 | Task process created |
| 141 | Task deleted |

Also check process creation logs after the task registration time for execution of the task action.

---

### Step 5
